blocks.content: Every Japanese verb belongs to one of three groups. The group determines *every* conjugation rule — get it right and the rest is predictable.

items: **Group 1 — Godan (五段):** ends in any う-column sound — く, ぐ, す, つ, ぬ, ぶ, む, う, or る*. The stem changes shape across forms following phonetic patterns.
**Group 2 — Ichidan (一段):** ends in る, with an い or え vowel immediately before it. The stem never changes — you only remove the る.
**Group 3 — Irregular:** only する (to do) and くる (to come). Both must be memorised.

blocks.content: る-ending Group 1 verbs look identical to Group 2 in dictionary form. 帰る (kaeru), 走る (hashiru), 知る (shiru), 切る (kiru) are all Group 1. There is no reliable visual test — when in doubt, check a dictionary. Recognition comes with exposure.

The **ます form** is how you speak politely. It is the default for conversations with people you do not know well, in formal situations, and in service environments. It covers both present habit and future intention — Japanese does not separate these two ideas.
Formation

groups.label: Group 1
groups.rule: change the final u-vowel to i-vowel, then add ます
groups.note: Negative: replace ます with ません — the stem stays the same
groups.description: The most common group — the majority of Japanese verbs fall here.

groups.label: Group 2
groups.rule: remove る, add ます directly to the stem
groups.description: Fewer verbs, but much simpler to conjugate.

groups.label: Group 3
groups.description: Only two verbs in Japanese are truly irregular — memorise them as-is.

rows.japanese: 毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。

blocks.content: ます covers both habits and planned future actions. Context makes the meaning clear — Japanese has no separate future tense.

ます is polite but not formal. Use it with a shop clerk, a new acquaintance, or a teacher. Among close friends, speakers drop to the plain (dictionary) form. Both are grammatically correct — register determines which fits.
The past tense is formed by replacing **ます** with **ました**. The negative past uses **ませんでした**. Both follow the same stem rules as the present tense — there is nothing new to memorise for the stem.

lines: Affirmative past: [stem] + **ました**
Negative past:    [stem] + **ませんでした**

rows.japanese: 朝ごはんを食べませんでした。
先週、東京に行きました。
rows.english: I went to Tokyo last week.

rows.japanese: レポートを書きませんでした。

blocks.content: Japanese past tense is clean — no distinction between simple past ("I ate") and perfect ("I have eaten") in the polite form. Time words and context carry that distinction.

Both **へ** and **に** can mark a destination when paired with a movement verb. They are often interchangeable, but each has a different focus: へ points at the direction of travel, に points at the arrival point. In everyday speech, に is more common.

lines: [Place] へ + [movement verb]   ← focus on the direction, the journey
[Place] に + [movement verb]   ← focus on the destination, arrival

rows.japanese: 駅のほうへ歩きました。
日本に引っ越しました。

blocks.content: に is required — not interchangeable with へ — with arrival verbs like 着く (to arrive) and 帰る (to return). These verbs already imply reaching a point, so に locks in the destination. 家に帰る = arrive back home. 家へ帰る = head toward home.
**で** marks *where an action takes place* — the venue or instrument of an activity. This is different from に, which marks *where something exists*. The verb is what tells you which particle to use.

lines: [Place] で + [action verb]   ← an action happens here
[Place] に + [existence verb] ← something exists here (います / あります)

rows.english: I read books on the train.

rows.japanese: 日本語で話してください。

left.label: で — action
left.description: Where something happens. Use with action verbs — running, studying, eating.

right.label: に — existence
right.description: Where something is. Use with います and あります — existing, being.

blocks.content: で vs に for location is one of the most common early errors. The verb tells you which to use: action verbs → で, existence verbs (います/あります) → に.

lessons.title: いる and ある — Existence

blocks.content: Japanese uses two different verbs to express "there is" or "to be," and the choice depends entirely on what kind of thing exists. **いる** is for living things. **ある** is for everything else.

lines: [Living thing] が [Place] に います   → there is/are (animate)
[Object/thing] が [Place] に あります  → there is/are (inanimate)

left.label: います
left.description: People, animals — anything that moves under its own power.
left.example_en: There is a cat in the room.

right.label: あります
right.description: Objects, plants, buildings, and even scheduled events like meetings.
right.example_jp: 本が机の上にあります。
right.example_en: There is a book on the desk.

rows.japanese: 駅の前に銀行があります。
rows.romaji: Eki no mae ni ginkō ga arimasu.
rows.english: There's a bank in front of the station.

rows.japanese: 財布がバッグの中にあります。
rows.romaji: Saifu ga baggu no naka ni arimasu.
rows.english: My wallet is inside the bag.

blocks.content: あります is used for scheduled events too — 会議があります (there's a meeting), 授業があります (there's a class). Events are treated as inanimate things that exist on the calendar.
Using ある for people — 友達が外にある — sounds wrong at best and rude at worst. The animate/inanimate distinction is instinctive for native speakers.
Japanese numbers are straightforward up to 10,000. The same digits combine and stack to form larger values — 十一 is 10+1, 百二十三 is 100+20+3. Learn the base set and the rest follows.
4 (し) and 9 (く) are avoided in some contexts — し sounds like 死 (death) and く like 苦 (suffering). Hospital rooms sometimes skip these numbers. This is cultural awareness, not grammar.
Japanese does not use bare numbers to count objects. Numbers pair with **counters** — suffixes that classify what is being counted. The number reading also changes depending on which counter follows.

lines: [Number] + [Counter]
三人 (sannin)   — three people
二枚 (nimai)    — two sheets
一杯 (ippai)    — one cup

rows.japanese: りんごを二個買いました。

rows.english: Please give me one sheet of paper.

rows.japanese: コーヒーを一杯飲みました。
rows.english: I drank one cup of coffee.

rows.japanese: 車を二台持っています。

blocks.content: Number + counter combinations trigger phonetic changes. 一本 (ippon), 三本 (sanbon), 六本 (roppon) — the pattern follows Japanese sound rules. Don't try to memorise all variants at once. Learn the counter first and pick up the sound changes through exposure.

lessons.title: Asking How Many — いくつ / 何～

blocks.content: There are two ways to ask "how many" in Japanese. Use **いくつ** when the category is unspecified or you want a general count. Use **何** (なん) directly before the counter when the category is already known.

left.label: いくつ
left.description: General count — used when the category is unspecified, or for things without a fixed counter.
left.example_jp: りんごがいくつありますか。

right.label: 何 + counter
right.description: Category-specific — attach 何 (nan) directly before the counter you would normally use.

rows.english: How many books did you read?

blocks.content: いくつ is also used informally to ask someone's age — お子さんはいくつですか (How old is your child?). The direct "how old" question is 何歳 (nansai).
Time in Japanese is stated with **時** (じ, hour) and **分** (ふん/ぷん, minute). The structure is simple: hour first, then minute, then です. AM and PM go before the time.

lines: [Hour] 時 [Minute] 分 です
ごぜん (AM) / ごご (PM) + [Hour] 時 [Minute] 分

rows.japanese: 九時十五分に始まります。
十二時半に昼ごはんを食べます。
rows.romaji: Jūniji han ni hirugohan wo tabemasu.

blocks.content: 半 (はん) means "half past" — 三時半 = 3:30. ごぜん and ごご come *before* the time: 午前九時 = 9 AM, 午後三時 = 3 PM. Without them, meaning comes from context.
Minute readings change based on the number. 一分 (ippun), 三分 (sanpun), 六分 (roppun), 八分 (happun), 十分 (juppun). These follow the same phonetic rules as counters — they become natural through listening.

lessons.title: Time Particles — に, から, まで

blocks.content: Three particles handle time relationships. **に** pins an action to a specific point — at a clock time or calendar date. **から** marks a start point. **まで** marks an end point. から and まで are often paired.

lines: [Specific time] に + [action]          ← at a specific time
[Start] から [End] まで + [action]     ← from A until B
[Start] から + [action]                ← from / since A (no end given)

rows.japanese: 月曜日に病院へ行きます。
rows.english: I go to the hospital on Monday.

rows.japanese: 九時から五時まで働きます。
授業は十時から始まります。
去年から日本語を勉強しています。
rows.romaji: Kyonen kara nihongo wo benkyō shite imasu.
rows.english: I've been studying Japanese since last year.

blocks.content: に is **not** used with relative time words like 今日, 明日, 毎日, 来週. These words are already time-referencing and don't need に. Say 明日行きます — never 明日**に**行きます. Think of に as "at a specific clock or calendar point." If the word is relative, drop the に.
These words are the building blocks of everyday temporal reference. None of them take the particle に — they are inherently time-referencing on their own.
Days
Weeks, Months, Years
Frequency
**い-adjectives** end in い and conjugate directly — the い changes to signal tense and polarity. They can modify nouns directly and stand as predicates without any additional linking word.

rows.japanese: 子どもの頃、背が高かったです。
rows.romaji: Kodomo no koro, se ga takakatta desu.
rows.english: I was tall as a child.

rows.japanese: 昨日の映画は長くなかったです。
rows.romaji: Kinō no eiga wa nagakunakatta desu.

blocks.content: いい (good) is irregular. Its negative is よくない (not いくない) and its past is よかった (not いかった). This is the single most common い-adjective error for beginners.
**な-adjectives** behave more like nouns than adjectives. They need **な** when directly modifying a noun, but conjugate by changing the following です — the adjective stem itself never changes.

left.label: Before a noun
left.description: Insert な between the adjective and the noun it modifies.

right.label: As a predicate
right.description: Use + です directly. No な needed after the adjective.

rows.japanese: 静かじゃなかったです

rows.romaji: Kanojo wa shinsetsu na hito desu.

rows.japanese: 部屋はきれいじゃないです。
rows.romaji: Heya wa kirei ja nai desu.

rows.japanese: この仕事は大変でした。

blocks.content: Not all adjectives ending in い are い-adjectives. きれい (beautiful), きらい (disliked), ゆうめい (famous) are all な-adjectives — they end in the *sound* い but conjugate like な-adjectives. When in doubt, check a dictionary.
To describe something with two or more qualities, connect adjectives using their **て-form**. The rule differs by adjective type: い-adjectives use くて, な-adjectives use で.

lines: い-adjective: [stem] + くて + [next clause]
安い  → 安くて
面白い → 面白くて
な-adjective: [な-adj] + で + [next clause]
静か → 静かで
便利 → 便利で

rows.english: It's a quiet and spacious room.

rows.japanese: この映画は長くてつまらなかったです。
rows.romaji: Kono eiga wa nagakute tsumaranakatta desu.
rows.english: This movie was long and boring.

rows.japanese: 彼女は親切で頭がいいです。
rows.romaji: Kanojo wa shinsetsu de atama ga ii desu.

blocks.content: The chained form expresses a neutral list — "X and Y" — not a causal connection. To say "it's cheap *so* I'll buy it," use から or ので, not くて.

lessons.title: から vs ので — Because

blocks.content: Both **から** and **ので** translate as "because," but they carry different weight. から states a reason directly and assertively. ので presents a reason as soft and objective — the natural consequence of a situation. Register and relationship determine which fits.

left.label: から
left.description: Assertive and personal — "my reason is X." Casual, direct. Use with friends or when stating feelings.

right.label: ので
right.description: Soft and objective — "given that X, naturally Y." Polite and indirect. Use for requests, apologies, workplace.
right.example_jp: 雨が降っているので、家にいます。
right.example_en: I'm staying home because it's raining.

lines: [Reason — plain form] + から、[Result]   ← subjective, casual
[Reason — plain form] + ので、[Result]   ← objective, polite

rows.japanese: 急いでいるから、あとで話しましょう。
rows.romaji: Isoide iru kara, ato de hanashimashō.
rows.english: I'm in a hurry, so let's talk later.

rows.japanese: 明日試験があるので、勉強します。
rows.romaji: Ashita shiken ga aru node, benkyō shimasu.
rows.english: I have an exam tomorrow, so I'll study.

rows.japanese: お腹が痛いので、休んでもいいですか。
rows.romaji: Onaka ga itai node, yasunde mo ii desu ka.
rows.english: My stomach hurts, so may I rest?

blocks.content: When making a polite request or excuse, ので always sounds more appropriate. 電車が遅れたので遅刻しました sounds like a genuine explanation. 電車が遅れたから遅刻しました sounds like a blunt justification. Same facts, different tone.

Japanese **question words** (疑問詞) slot into the sentence exactly where the unknown information would go. The rest of the sentence structure stays the same — there is no subject-verb inversion like in English.

rows.japanese: どんな音楽が好きですか。
rows.romaji: Donna ongaku ga suki desu ka.
rows.english: What kind of music do you like?

rows.japanese: なぜ日本語を勉強していますか。
rows.romaji: Naze nihongo wo benkyō shite imasu ka.

blocks.content: 何 reads as なに before most words, but switches to なん before sounds starting with t, d, or n — and before counters. 何時 (nanji), 何人 (nannin), 何番 (nanban). The switch is phonetic, not grammatical.
Question words in Japanese cannot combine with は (topic particle). 誰**は** and どこ**は** are ungrammatical. Use が for subjects: 誰が来ましたか. Use を for objects: 何を食べましたか.
**間** expresses a span of time — how long something lasted or how long an action continued. It attaches directly after the duration amount.

lines: [Duration] + 間 + [action / state]
三時間   (sanjikan)    — for three hours
一週間   (isshūkan)    — for one week
二年間   (ninenkan)    — for two years
十分間   (juppunkan)   — for ten minutes

rows.japanese: 一週間日本にいました。
rows.english: I was in Japan for one week.

rows.japanese: 二年間日本語を学んでいます。
rows.english: I have been learning Japanese for two years.

blocks.content: 間 has two readings. Combined with numbers it reads **かん** (三時間, 一週間). Used alone or in short phrases it can read **あいだ** (この間 = recently, the other day). In duration expressions, かん is almost always correct.
**回** (かい) counts the number of times something occurs. Pair it with a time frame and a number to express how often an action happens.

lines: [Time period] に [number] 回 + [action]
週に三回    — three times a week
一日に二回  — twice a day
月に一度    — once a month (一度 = one time, softer alternative to 一回)

rows.japanese: 週に三回ジムに行きます。
rows.romaji: Shū ni sankai jimu ni ikimasu.
rows.english: I go to the gym three times a week.

rows.japanese: 一日に二回薬を飲みます。
rows.romaji: Ichinichi ni nikai kusuri wo nomimasu.
rows.english: I take medicine twice a day.

rows.japanese: 月に一度、家族に電話します。
rows.romaji: Tsuki ni ichido, kazoku ni denwa shimasu.
rows.english: I call my family once a month.

rows.japanese: 年に一回しか会いません。
rows.english: We only meet once a year.

blocks.content: 回 triggers phonetic changes with certain numbers. 一回 (ikkai), 六回 (rokkai), 八回 (hakkai), 十回 (jukkai) — a geminate っ appears before k. You will pick these up naturally from listening; don't memorise the full table upfront.
**かかる** is the verb for expressing that something *requires* a certain amount of time or money. It is not used for effort or energy — only for measurable time and cost.

lines: [Time / cost] が かかります     ← it takes / it costs
[Destination] まで [time] かかります  ← it takes [time] to reach
どのぐらいかかりますか           ← how long / how much does it take?

rows.japanese: 駅まで十分かかります。
rows.english: It takes ten minutes to the station.

rows.japanese: この仕事は三時間かかりました。
修理に五千円かかりました。
日本までどのぐらいかかりますか。
rows.romaji: Nihon made dono gurai kakarimasu ka.
rows.english: How long does it take to get to Japan?

rows.japanese: このプロジェクトはお金がかかります。
rows.romaji: Kono purojekuto wa okane ga kakarimasu.

blocks.content: かかる pairs naturally with まで (up to / until). 駅まで何分かかりますか is the most natural way to ask travel time in Japanese — you will use it constantly.
**たい** attaches to the verb stem and expresses the speaker's personal desire to do something. It conjugates exactly like an い-adjective — the same stem changes apply.

lines: [Verb stem] + たいです        (want to do)
[Verb stem] + たくないです    (don't want to do)
[Verb stem] + たかったです    (wanted to do)

rows.english: I want to go to Japan.

rows.japanese: 今日は外出したくないです。
rows.english: I don't want to go out today.
What do you want to eat?

rows.japanese: 子どもの頃、医者になりたかったです。
rows.romaji: Kodomo no koro, isha ni naritakatta desu.
rows.english: When I was a child, I wanted to become a doctor.

blocks.content: The direct object of たい often takes が instead of を — 寿司**が**食べたい sounds slightly more natural than 寿司**を**食べたい, though both are correct. Think of が as pairing the desire with its target.
たい describes *your own* desire. Saying 田中さんは行きたい directly implies you know their inner feelings, which can sound presumptuous. For third-person desire, use 田中さんは行きたがっている (seems to want to go).
**ほしい** expresses desire for a *thing* — a noun, not an action. It is an い-adjective and conjugates the same way. The object is always marked with が.

lines: [Object] が ほしいです        (want something)
[Object] が ほしくないです    (don't want something)
[Object] が ほしかったです    (wanted something)

left.label: たい — action
left.description: Attaches to a verb stem. Expresses the desire to *do* something.

right.label: ほしい — object
right.description: Follows a noun with が. Expresses the desire to *have* something.
right.example_jp: 新しいカメラがほしいです。

rows.japanese: 新しいカメラがほしいです。
今は何もほしくないです。
rows.romaji: Ima wa nani mo hoshikunai desu.
rows.english: I don't want anything right now.

rows.japanese: 子どもの頃、犬がほしかったです。
rows.romaji: Kodomo no koro, inu ga hoshikatta desu.
rows.english: When I was a child, I wanted a dog.

blocks.content: ほしい carries the same register restriction as たい — use it for your own desires only. For someone else wanting something, say ほしがっている (seems to want).

lessons.title: Probability — でしょう / かもしれない

blocks.content: These two forms express degrees of certainty about something unconfirmed. **でしょう** is fairly confident — the speaker's informed expectation. **かもしれない** is genuinely uncertain — the speaker is leaving room for doubt.

left.label: でしょう
left.description: Probably — the speaker is fairly confident. Based on evidence or reasoning.
left.example_jp: 明日は晴れるでしょう。
left.example_en: It will probably be sunny tomorrow.

right.label: かもしれない
right.description: Might — the speaker is genuinely uncertain. Real possibility but not expected.
right.example_jp: 彼は来ないかもしれません。

lines: [Plain form] + でしょう          ← probably (fairly confident)
[Plain form] + かもしれません    ← might (uncertain)

rows.japanese: このレストランは高いでしょう。
電車が遅れているかもしれません。
rows.romaji: Densha ga okurete iru kamo shiremasen.
rows.english: The train might be running late.

rows.japanese: 彼女はもう知っているでしょう。
rows.romaji: Kanojo wa mō shitte iru deshō.

rows.japanese: 明日、雨が降るかもしれません。
rows.romaji: Ashita, ame ga furu kamo shiremasen.

blocks.content: でしょう with a rising intonation becomes a soft question tag — そうでしょう？ means "That's right, isn't it?" / "Don't you think?" This is a completely separate use from the probability meaning.

The **て-form** is one of the most versatile verb forms in Japanese. It acts as a connector between clauses and is the base for dozens of grammar patterns. Mastering it early pays off through all of N5 and beyond.

groups.label: Group 1
groups.rule: く → いて / ぐ → いで
groups.note: Exception: 行く → 行って (not 行いて)

blocks.content: 行く (to go) is the one Group 1 exception — it becomes 行って, not 行いて. Everything else follows the cards above without exception.
The most direct and natural way to make a polite request is **て-form + ください**. It is appropriate in almost any polite context — shops, classrooms, public signs.

lines: [て-form] + ください   ← please do ~

rows.japanese: ここに名前を書いてください。
rows.romaji: Koko ni namae wo kaite kudasai.

rows.japanese: もう一度言ってください。
rows.english: Please say it one more time.

rows.japanese: 右に曲がってください。

blocks.content: Register options: drop ください entirely for casual requests — 書いて means "write this" among friends. Use ていただけますか for more deferential situations, like addressing a superior or making a formal request.
Two て-form patterns cover what is and is not allowed. **てもいいです** gives permission or asks for it. **てはいけません** states that something is not permitted.

lines: [て-form] + もいいです      ← it is okay to / you may
[て-form] + もいいですか    ← may I / is it okay to?
[て-form] + はいけません    ← you must not / it is not allowed

rows.japanese: ここで写真を撮ってもいいですか。
rows.romaji: Koko de shashin wo totte mo ii desu ka.

rows.japanese: 窓を開けてもいいですよ。
rows.romaji: Mado wo akete mo ii desu yo.

rows.japanese: ここでタバコを吸ってはいけません。
rows.romaji: Koko de tabako wo sutte wa ikemasen.

rows.japanese: 試験中にスマホを使ってはいけません。
rows.romaji: Shiken chū ni sumaho wo tsukatte wa ikemasen.
rows.english: You must not use your phone during the exam.

blocks.content: In casual speech, てもいいです shortens to ていい. てはいけない contracts to ちゃいけない (from ては → ちゃ). Both are common in everyday conversation but not appropriate in formal writing.
Japanese tracks the *direction* of a favour with precision. Three て-form patterns each handle one direction — outward from you, inward to you, or arriving unsolicited.

items: **てあげる** — I (or someone) do something *for* someone else. The benefit flows outward.
**てもらう** — I receive an action *from* someone. I am the beneficiary, often having asked.
**てくれる** — Someone does something for me on their own initiative. The benefit arrives without me requesting it.

lines: [て-form] + あげます   ← I do for them (benefit flows out)
[て-form] + もらいます ← I receive the action (benefit flows in)
[て-form] + くれます   ← they do for me, their initiative

rows.japanese: 友達の荷物を持ってあげました。
rows.romaji: Tomodachi no nimotsu wo motte agemashita.
rows.english: I carried my friend's bags for them.

rows.japanese: 先生に漢字を教えてもらいました。
rows.romaji: Sensei ni kanji wo oshiete moraimashita.
rows.english: I had the teacher teach me kanji.

rows.japanese: 母が弁当を作ってくれました。
rows.romaji: Haha ga bentō wo tsukutte kuremashita.
rows.english: My mother made me a bento (for my benefit).

rows.japanese: 田中さんが駅まで送ってくれました。
rows.romaji: Tanaka-san ga eki made okutte kuremashita.
rows.english: Tanaka kindly drove me to the station.

blocks.content: The key question: *who is the beneficiary?* Benefit goes to someone else → あげる. Benefit comes to me, I requested it → もらう. Benefit comes to me, their own initiative → くれる.

lessons.title: ている — Ongoing Action and State

blocks.content: **ている** is one of the most frequently used patterns in Japanese. The same form carries three distinct meanings — context and the verb itself determine which reading applies.

items: **In progress** — an action happening right now, like English "-ing"
**Resultant state** — the lasting result of a completed action
**Habitual** — something done regularly as a routine

lines: [て-form] + います

rows.english: I am reading a book now.

rows.japanese: 彼女は結婚しています。
田中さんはあそこに座っています。
rows.romaji: Tanaka-san wa asoko ni suwatte imasu.

blocks.content: The resultant-state meaning catches learners who expect ている to always mean "currently doing." 結婚しています = "is in a married state," not "is getting married right now." 知っています = "I know" (not "I am knowing"). 着ています = "is wearing" (the result of having put it on).
**てから** expresses a strict sequence: action A must be fully completed before action B can begin. The completion of A is what makes B possible or appropriate.

lines: [て-form] + から、[next action]

rows.japanese: 手を洗ってから、食べます。
rows.english: I eat after washing my hands.

rows.japanese: 宿題をしてから、ゲームをします。
rows.romaji: Shukudai wo shite kara, gēmu wo shimasu.
rows.english: I play games after doing homework.

rows.japanese: 大学を卒業してから、働き始めました。
rows.romaji: Daigaku wo sotsugyō shite kara, hataraki hajimemashita.
rows.english: I started working after graduating from university.

rows.japanese: シャワーを浴びてから、寝ます。
rows.english: I sleep after taking a shower.

left.label: てから
left.description: A must be fully done before B. Completion is required — the sequence is strict.
left.example_jp: 食べてから、歯を磨きます。
left.example_en: I brush my teeth after eating.

right.label: 後で
right.description: "Later, after A" — B happens sometime after, with no strict completion implied.

lessons.title: 前に / 後で — Before / After

blocks.content: **前に** and **後で** describe timing relative to another action. They are more flexible than てから — no strict completion is implied. The verb form before each one is different, and the reason is logical.

lines: [Dictionary form] + 前に、[action]       ← before doing (action hasn't happened yet)
[Past plain form] + 後で、[action]       ← after doing (action has been completed)
[Noun] + の前に / の後で                  ← before / after a noun (event, class, etc.)

rows.japanese: 寝る前に歯を磨きます。
rows.romaji: Neru mae ni ha wo migakimasu.
rows.english: I brush my teeth before sleeping.

rows.japanese: 食べた後で、散歩します。
rows.english: I take a walk after eating.

rows.japanese: 授業の前に、単語を復習しました。
rows.romaji: Jugyō no mae ni, tango wo fukushū shimashita.

rows.japanese: 映画の後で、カフェに行きましょう。
rows.romaji: Eiga no ato de, kafe ni ikimashō.
rows.english: Let's go to a café after the movie.

blocks.content: 前に takes the dictionary form because the action has *not yet happened* at that point in time — it is still in the future relative to the reference moment. 後で takes the past plain form because the action *has been completed* before the next one starts.

**ながら** attaches to the verb stem to describe two actions happening simultaneously. The ながら clause is always the *secondary* action — the main verb at the end of the sentence is what the subject is primarily doing.

lines: [Verb stem] + ながら、[main action]
聴く  → 聴き + ながら
歩く  → 歩き + ながら
飲む  → 飲み + ながら

rows.japanese: 音楽を聴きながら勉強します。
rows.english: I study while listening to music.

rows.japanese: 歩きながら電話で話しました。
rows.english: I talked on the phone while walking.

rows.japanese: テレビを見ながら夕ごはんを食べます。
rows.romaji: Terebi wo minagara yūgohan wo tabemasu.
rows.english: I eat dinner while watching TV.

rows.japanese: コーヒーを飲みながら新聞を読みました。
rows.romaji: Koohii wo nominagara shinbun wo yomimashita.
rows.english: I read the newspaper while drinking coffee.

blocks.content: ながら requires the *same subject* for both actions. "I study while she watches TV" cannot use ながら — a different subject performing the secondary action requires a different structure.

lessons.title: A は B より ～ — More Than

blocks.content: **より** marks the baseline of comparison — what you are comparing *against*. What comes before より is the lesser item; what comes before the adjective is the greater one.

lines: A は B より [adjective] です       ← A is more ~ than B
B より A のほうが [adjective] です  ← A is more ~ than B (emphatic)

rows.japanese: 東京は大阪より大きいです。
rows.romaji: Tōkyō wa Ōsaka yori ōkii desu.

rows.japanese: バスより電車のほうが速いです。
rows.romaji: Basu yori densha no hō ga hayai desu.
rows.english: The train is faster than the bus.

rows.japanese: 夏より冬のほうが好きです。
rows.romaji: Natsu yori fuyu no hō ga suki desu.

rows.japanese: 昨日より今日のほうが寒いです。
rows.romaji: Kinō yori kyō no hō ga samui desu.

rows.japanese: 肉より魚のほうが好きです。
rows.romaji: Niku yori sakana no hō ga suki desu.
rows.english: I like fish more than meat.

blocks.content: Adding のほうが after the item being elevated makes the comparison more explicit and emphatic. Both structures are grammatically correct — のほうが is simply more common in natural speech.

lessons.title: どちらが ～ — Which is More ~?

blocks.content: To ask which of **two** things has a quality more than the other, use **どちら** (or どっち in casual speech) before が. The answer uses のほうが to identify the winner, or どちらも when both are equal.

lines: A と B と どちらが [adjective] ですか   ← which is more ~?
→ A のほうが [adjective] です         ← A is more ~
→ どちらも [adjective] です           ← both are equally ~

rows.japanese: 犬と猫とどちらが好きですか。
rows.romaji: Inu to neko to dochira ga suki desu ka.
rows.english: Which do you like more, dogs or cats?

rows.romaji: Neko no hō ga suki desu.

rows.japanese: コーヒーと紅茶とどちらを飲みますか。
rows.romaji: Koohii to kōcha to dochira wo nomimasu ka.
rows.english: Which would you like, coffee or tea?

rows.japanese: 電車とバスとどちらが便利ですか。
rows.romaji: Densha to basu to dochira ga benri desu ka.
rows.english: Which is more convenient, the train or the bus?

blocks.content: どちら is the polite form; どっち is casual and more common in everyday conversation. Use どちら with people you don't know well or in formal situations.
**いちばん** (一番) means "number one" and acts as a superlative marker. It goes directly before the adjective or adverb — no change to the adjective itself.

lines: [Group] の中で、[item] が いちばん [adjective] です
の中で (no naka de) = "among" — optional but common

rows.japanese: クラスで田中さんが一番背が高いです。
rows.romaji: Kurasu de Tanaka-san ga ichiban se ga takai desu.
rows.english: Tanaka is the tallest in the class.

rows.japanese: 日本で一番高い山は富士山です。
rows.romaji: Nihon de ichiban takai yama wa Fujisan desu.
rows.english: Mt. Fuji is the tallest mountain in Japan.

rows.japanese: 何の科目がいちばん好きですか。
rows.romaji: Nani no kamoku ga ichiban suki desu ka.
rows.english: Which subject do you like the most?

rows.japanese: このメニューの中で一番安い料理はどれですか。
rows.romaji: Kono menyū no naka de ichiban yasui ryōri wa dore desu ka.
rows.english: Which dish on this menu is the cheapest?

rows.japanese: 世界で一番大きい国はどこですか。
rows.romaji: Sekai de ichiban ōkii kuni wa doko desu ka.
rows.english: Which is the largest country in the world?

blocks.content: いちばん can modify adjectives (一番高い), adverbs (一番速く), and nouns when paired with suki/kirai (一番好きな食べ物). It is one of the simplest patterns at N5 — the adjective needs no modification at all.

lessons.title: たほうがいい — Should / Shouldn't

blocks.content: **たほうがいい** expresses advice — suggesting that a course of action would be in the listener's best interest. The affirmative uses the past plain form; the negative uses the negative plain form.

lines: [Past plain] + ほうがいいです       ← you should do
[Negative plain] + ほうがいいです   ← you shouldn't do

rows.japanese: 早く寝たほうがいいです。
rows.romaji: Hayaku neta hō ga ii desu.

rows.japanese: タバコを吸わないほうがいいです。
rows.romaji: Tabako wo suwanai hō ga ii desu.

rows.japanese: 傘を持っていったほうがいいですよ。
rows.romaji: Kasa wo motte itta hō ga ii desu yo.

rows.japanese: 無理をしないほうがいいです。
rows.romaji: Muri wo shinai hō ga ii desu.
rows.english: You shouldn't push yourself too hard.

blocks.content: たほうがいい is advice, not a command. It signals that the speaker genuinely thinks this is in the listener's interest. For stronger obligation, use なければなりません.
Two patterns cover what is required and what is not. **なければなりません** states that something must be done. **なくてもいいです** is its inverse — the action is not required.

left.label: なければなりません
left.description: Must do — the action is an obligation. Formal, used in writing and polite speech.
left.example_jp: 薬を毎日飲まなければなりません。
left.example_en: I have to take medicine every day.

right.label: なくてもいいです
right.description: Don't have to — the action is optional. Giving permission not to do something.
right.example_jp: 今日は来なくてもいいです。
right.example_en: You don't have to come today.

lines: [Neg. stem] + なければなりません   ← must (formal / polite)
[Neg. stem] + ないといけません     ← must (casual spoken)
[Neg. te-form] + もいいです        ← don't have to

rows.japanese: 明日までにレポートを出さなければなりません。
rows.romaji: Ashita made ni repōto wo dasanakereba narimasen.
rows.english: I must submit the report by tomorrow.

rows.japanese: もっと練習しないといけません。
全部食べなくてもいいですよ。
rows.romaji: Zenbu tabenakute mo ii desu yo.
rows.english: You don't have to eat everything.

rows.japanese: ネクタイをしなくてもいいです。
rows.romaji: Nekutai wo shinakute mo ii desu.
rows.english: You don't need to wear a tie.

blocks.content: なきゃ and なくちゃ are heavily contracted casual forms of なければならない — you will hear them constantly in everyday speech and anime. They are not appropriate in formal writing.

lessons.title: と思います — I Think That

blocks.content: **と思います** expresses personal opinion or belief. The と marks the boundary of the thought being reported. It makes statements sound appropriately tentative — stating something flatly without it can feel blunt.

lines: [Plain form] + と思います   ← I think that ~

rows.japanese: 明日は雨が降ると思います。
rows.romaji: Ashita wa ame ga furu to omoimasu.
rows.english: I think it will rain tomorrow.

rows.japanese: 彼は来ないと思います。
この映画は面白いと思います。
rows.romaji: Kono eiga wa omoshiroi to omoimasu.
rows.english: I think this movie is interesting.

rows.japanese: もう少し考えたほうがいいと思います。
rows.romaji: Mō sukoshi kangaeta hō ga ii to omoimasu.
rows.english: I think you should think it over a bit more.

blocks.content: The clause before と is always in the **plain form**, not the polite form. 来ます**と**思います is wrong — it should be 来る**と**思います. The politeness is carried by the final と思います alone.

lessons.title: つもり & 予定 — Intention and Plans

blocks.content: Both **つもり** and **予定** express future plans, but they differ in who made the decision and how fixed it is.

left.label: つもりです
left.description: Personal intention — an internal decision already made in your own mind. Not dependent on others.
left.example_jp: 来年、日本に行くつもりです。
left.example_en: I intend to go to Japan next year.

right.label: 予定です
right.description: Scheduled plan — often external, fixed, or coordinated with others. Suits appointments and timetables.
right.example_jp: 三時に会議が始まる予定です。
right.example_en: The meeting is scheduled to start at 3.

lines: [Dictionary form] + つもりです      ← intend to (personal decision)
[Negative plain] + つもりです       ← intend not to
[Dictionary form] + 予定です        ← scheduled to (arranged plan)
[Noun] + の + 予定です              ← have a plan for ~

rows.japanese: もうお酒を飲まないつもりです。
rows.romaji: Mō osake wo nomanai tsumori desu.
rows.english: I intend not to drink anymore.
I have a business trip planned next month.

rows.japanese: 飛行機は六時に到着する予定です。
rows.romaji: Hikōki wa rokuji ni tōchaku suru yotei desu.
rows.english: The plane is scheduled to arrive at 6.

blocks.content: If you made a reservation or appointment, use 予定. If you have decided something for yourself regardless of others, use つもり.

**んです** (written のです) adds an explanatory nuance to a statement. It signals that what you are saying is the reason behind something, the context for a situation, or a request for explanation — not just a bare fact.

lines: [Plain form verb / い-adj] + んです
[な-adj / noun] + な + んです

rows.japanese: どうして遅れたんですか。
rows.english: Why were you late? (explain it to me)

rows.japanese: 実は、昨日転んだんです。
rows.romaji: Jitsu wa, kinō koronda n desu.
rows.english: The thing is, I fell yesterday.

rows.japanese: ちょっと聞いてもいいんですが…
rows.romaji: Chotto kiite mo ii n desu ga…
rows.english: I was wondering if I could ask you something…

blocks.content: Without んです, 頭が痛いです is a plain statement of fact. With it, 頭が痛いんです implies "I'm telling you this because it's relevant — that's why I look unwell / can't attend." Use it when you want to signal context, not just information.
The kanji **中** attaches to nouns with two different readings and two different meanings. The verb or context usually makes the reading clear.

left.label: 〜中 (ちゅう)
left.description: Currently in that activity or state — happening right now.
left.example_en: I'm in a meeting right now.

right.label: 〜中 (じゅう)
right.description: Spanning the whole thing — throughout all of a time or space.
right.example_en: I've been working all day long.

rows.japanese: すみません、今、電話中です。
rows.english: Sorry, I'm on the phone right now.

rows.japanese: 使用中のため入れません。
世界中の人が知っています。
rows.romaji: Sekai jū no hito ga shitte imasu.
rows.english: People all over the world know about it.

rows.japanese: 日本中を旅行しました。

blocks.content: ちゅう = the activity is in progress right now (a slice of time). じゅう = no part is excluded (the full extent of a time or space). 勉強中 = studying at this moment. 一日中勉強した = studied without stopping for the entire day.
